introduction.heading: Describe the What, Not the How
introduction.description: A traditional loop spells out every mechanical step: make an index, check the bound, increment, pull an element, test it, add it to a result list. The Stream API lets you describe the outcome instead - "of these orders, keep the shipped ones, take their totals, add them up" - and leaves the stepping to the library. Lambdas are what make that readable: a lambda is just a short, unnamed function you pass as an argument, so `o -> o.isShipped()` is a throwaway test you hand to `filter`. Together they turn a page of nested loops into a pipeline you can read top to bottom. This lesson is about building that mental model - source, intermediate operations, terminal operation - and knowing when a plain loop is still the better call.

concepts.title: Lambda Expression
concepts.description: An anonymous function written inline: parameters -> body. `x -> x * 2` and `(a, b) -> a + b` are lambdas; they exist to be passed to a method, not stored and named

concepts.title: Functional Interface
concepts.description: An interface with exactly one abstract method - Predicate<T> (T -> boolean), Function<T,R> (T -> R), Consumer<T> (T -> void), Supplier<T> (() -> T). A lambda's shape has to match the one method

concepts.title: Method Reference
concepts.description: A shorthand for a lambda that just calls one existing method: String::toUpperCase instead of s -> s.toUpperCase(), Order::getTotal instead of o -> o.getTotal()

concepts.title: Stream Pipeline
concepts.description: A source (a collection, Stream.of, ...), zero or more intermediate operations (map, filter, sorted, distinct, limit) that each return a new stream, and exactly one terminal operation (collect, reduce, forEach, count) that produces a result or side effect

concepts.title: Laziness & Short-Circuiting
concepts.description: Intermediate operations do nothing until a terminal operation runs; then elements are pulled through one at a time. findFirst, anyMatch, and limit can stop early without touching the rest of the source

concepts.title: Collectors & Optional
concepts.description: Collectors.toList / groupingBy / partitioningBy / toMap turn a stream back into a data structure. Optional<T> is a box that holds a value or nothing - the return type of operations like findFirst that might have no answer, so a missing result is explicit instead of a null

pipeline.heading: A Pipeline, Element by Element
pipeline.description: The thing that trips people up first is imagining a stream runs each operation over the whole collection before moving to the next - filter everything, then map everything. It doesn't. Once the terminal operation starts, each element is drawn through the entire pipeline before the next element is touched, and nothing runs at all until that terminal operation is attached. Build a pipeline below and watch a single element travel through it.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Start the pipeline from a collection with .stream(), and remember a stream is single-use - you can't iterate it twice
Reach for a functional interface by shape: a test is a Predicate, a transform is a Function, 'do something with each' is a Consumer
Chain intermediate operations - filter to narrow, map to transform, sorted / distinct / limit to shape - each one returns a new stream
Finish with exactly one terminal operation; if there's no terminal operation, none of the pipeline runs
Prefer collect(Collectors.toList()) (or .toList() on Java 16+) over forEach + external list - it states the intent and avoids a shared mutable list
Use groupingBy when you'd otherwise build a Map<K, List<V>> by hand, and partitioningBy for a true/false split
Treat Optional as a pipeline of its own - map / filter / orElseGet - rather than calling .get() straight away
Reach back for a plain for loop when you need the index, have to mutate the source, or want to break out with a side effect - streams aren't a rule, they're a tool

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: Analyze a list of orders with one stream pipeline
fullExample.description: A single class that answers a few questions about a list of orders - total revenue from shipped orders, the biggest order per customer, a breakdown by status - using streams instead of nested loops. Click through the steps to see each pipeline and what its intermediate and terminal operations do.

steps.label: The data and the functional interfaces in play
steps.explanation: Order is a record, so getters are total(), status(), customer(). The methods below use Predicate (the filter tests), Function (the map / groupingBy classifiers) and a Comparator (built with Comparator.comparing, itself taking a Function).

steps.label: filter + mapToLong + sum: revenue from shipped orders
steps.explanation: filter keeps only SHIPPED orders; mapToLong turns each into a primitive long total (avoiding boxing); sum() is the terminal operation. No intermediate list is ever built - each order that passes the filter is added straight into the running sum.

steps.label: groupingBy with a downstream collector: biggest order per customer
steps.explanation: groupingBy(Order::customer, ...) buckets orders by customer; the second argument, maxBy(comparing(Order::total)), is a downstream collector applied within each bucket, so the result is Map<String, Optional<Order>> - the biggest order for each customer.

steps.label: groupingBy + counting: how many orders in each status
steps.explanation: The same shape again - classify by Order::status, and count within each group with Collectors.counting(). This one line replaces a Map<Status, Integer> that you'd otherwise create, getOrDefault, and increment by hand.

steps.label: findFirst returns an Optional, and laziness makes it cheap
steps.explanation: The pipeline is filter then findFirst. Because streams are lazy and findFirst short-circuits, the filter runs only until the first match is found - the rest of the list is never examined. The Optional return type forces the caller to say what happens when there's no unshipped order.

quiz.question: You write a stream pipeline: list.stream().filter(...).map(...). Nothing seems to happen. Why?
options: filter and map throw if the list is empty
There is no terminal operation, so the pipeline never runs
quiz.explanation: Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted...) are lazy - they only describe work. Nothing executes until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, count, reduce...) is attached.

quiz.question: Which functional interface does the lambda `s -> s.isBlank()` match?
quiz.explanation: It takes one argument and returns a boolean - that's Predicate<String>. A Function returns an arbitrary R, a Consumer returns void, a Supplier takes no argument.

quiz.question: What is the result type of `orders.stream().collect(groupingBy(Order::status))`?
quiz.explanation: groupingBy with just a classifier produces Map<K, List<V>> - each distinct key mapped to the list of elements that fell into it. A downstream collector (counting, mapping, maxBy...) changes the value type.

quiz.question: `people.stream().filter(p -> p.age() > 90).findFirst()` on a 10-million-element list where the 3rd person matches. Roughly how many elements are inspected?
quiz.explanation: findFirst short-circuits. Elements are pulled through filter one at a time and the stream stops as soon as findFirst has its answer - here after the 3rd element.

quiz.question: When is a plain for loop still the better choice over a stream?
options: When you need the index, must mutate the source in place, or want to break early with a side effect
Only for arrays, never for lists
When the collection has fewer than 100 elements
quiz.explanation: Streams shine for declarative transform-and-collect. Index-based logic, in-place mutation, and early exit with side effects are all more direct and readable as an ordinary loop.
